options.a: Treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious
options.b: Apply PPE and extra precautions for patients with a known bloodborne infection
options.c: Treat blood as infectious but handle saliva as noninfectious unless visibly bloody
options.d: Change gloves between patients but skip hand hygiene when gloves were worn

distractorExplanations.b: Precautions keyed to disclosed infection status are outdated; Standard Precautions apply to every patient because status is often unknown.
distractorExplanations.c: In dentistry saliva is treated as potentially infectious material; the bloody-saliva exception belongs to old Universal Precautions outside dentistry.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves can have micro-defects and hands get contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is still required after gloves come off.

danb-ice-readiness-check-standard-precau.explanation: Standard Precautions assume unknown infectious status; gloves do not replace hand hygiene. This includes using appropriate PPE and hand hygiene with every patient.

options.a: After removing gloves at the end of each patient, but not before gloving
options.b: Only when hands are visibly soiled, since glove use covers routine contact
options.c: Before donning gloves, after removing gloves, and whenever hands are contaminated
options.d: At the start and end of each shift, with glove changes covering patient contacts

distractorExplanations.a: Skips hand hygiene before donning gloves; unclean hands contaminate new gloves, so hygiene is required both before and after glove use.
distractorExplanations.b: Visible soil is the trigger for soap and water, not the only trigger; gloves never replace hand hygiene before and after patient care.
distractorExplanations.d: Shift-based hand hygiene ignores the per-patient moments around gloving; a glove change without hand hygiene leaves hands contaminated.

options.a: Gloves and a surgical mask, with eye protection reserved for the operator
options.b: Gloves and protective eyewear; a mask only when the patient reports a cough
options.c: Gloves, gown, and a face shield used in place of a mask and eyewear
options.d: Gloves, mask, and eye protection; gown when soiling of clothing is likely

distractorExplanations.a: The assistant sits in the same spatter zone as the operator, so eye protection is required for everyone exposed, not just the operator.
distractorExplanations.b: The mask protects the nose and mouth from blood/saliva splash on every spatter-generating procedure, not only for respiratory symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: A face shield can replace eyewear, but CDC still calls for a mask under it because spatter travels around the shield to the nose and mouth.

danb-ice-readiness-check-standard-precau.explanation: Mucous membrane and clothing protection match splash risk. Eye protection may be goggles or a face shield.

options.a: Protect hands during cleaning of contaminated instruments and handling chemicals
options.b: Serve as the sterile glove for minor surgical procedures after an autoclave cycle
options.c: Replace exam gloves for chairside patient care when a patient has a latex allergy
options.d: Be discarded after each use like exam gloves rather than washed and reused

distractorExplanations.b: Utility gloves are heavy puncture-resistant gloves for decontamination; surgical procedures require sterile surgical gloves.
distractorExplanations.c: Utility gloves are too bulky and are not patient-care gloves; a latex-allergic patient gets nitrile or other non-latex exam gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Unlike exam gloves, utility gloves may be cleaned, disinfected, and reused until they crack, tear, or show other signs of deterioration.

options.a: At the end of each half-day session if they still look intact
options.b: They become wet, soiled, or between patients per protocol
options.c: Once daily, after the last patient, unless visibly torn
options.d: When they become wet, but the same mask may be kept on for several patients

distractorExplanations.a: Session-based changes let one mask serve several patients; masks are changed between patients and whenever wet or soiled.
distractorExplanations.c: Daily changes ignore moisture buildup and cross-patient contamination; masks are changed per patient and when wet or soiled.
distractorExplanations.d: Getting wet is one trigger, but a mask is also changed between patients because its outer surface is contaminated by spatter.

options.a: Switch an allergic worker to powder-free latex gloves, which remove the allergy risk
options.b: Treat latex allergy like irritant dermatitis, managed with hand lotion and glove liners
options.c: Use non-latex alternatives when indicated and minimize unnecessary latex powder exposures
options.d: Screen patients for latex allergy but leave staff glove choice to personal preference

distractorExplanations.a: Powder-free latex cuts airborne allergen but still contains latex proteins; an allergic worker needs non-latex gloves such as nitrile.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses immune-mediated latex allergy (Type I or IV) with irritant contact dermatitis; lotion and liners do not stop the allergic reaction.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA requires employers to provide non-latex or hypoallergenic alternatives to allergic employees; staff allergy is not left to preference.

options.a: Instruments that penetrate soft tissue or bone
options.b: Mouth mirrors that touch mucous membranes
options.c: Amalgam condensers that contact oral tissue
options.d: Radiograph positioning devices placed in the mouth

distractorExplanations.b: Mouth mirrors contact mucosa without penetrating tissue, which makes them semicritical items under the Spaulding classification.
distractorExplanations.c: CDC lists amalgam condensers as semicritical: they touch mucous membranes but do not penetrate soft tissue or bone.
distractorExplanations.d: Intraoral film/sensor holders contact mucous membranes only, so they are semicritical (heat-sterilize or high-level disinfect).

danb-ice-readiness-check-standard-precau.explanation: Critical items contact sterile tissue/vasculature and require sterilization. Examples include surgical instruments and periodontal scalers.

options.a: Cleaned and wiped with an intermediate-level surface disinfectant between patients
options.b: Heat-sterilized when heat-tolerant; if heat-sensitive, use high-level disinfection
options.c: Sterilized only when they penetrate tissue; otherwise low-level disinfection suffices
options.d: Soaked in a high-level disinfectant as the first choice even when heat-tolerant

distractorExplanations.a: Intermediate-level disinfectants are for clinical contact surfaces and noncritical items; semicritical items need sterilization or HLD.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses semicritical with noncritical: low-level disinfection is for intact-skin items, while mucosal-contact items need sterilization or HLD.
distractorExplanations.d: CDC prefers heat sterilization for heat-tolerant semicritical items; chemical HLD is reserved for items that cannot withstand heat.

danb-ice-readiness-check-standard-precau.explanation: Semicritical items need sterilization or HLD depending on material tolerance. Follow the manufacturer's IFU for heat-sensitive items.

options.a: After each patient by washing gloved hands, changing them only when torn
options.b: At the start and end of each session, unless a tear becomes visible
options.c: Between patients and whenever torn/contaminated during a procedure
options.d: Between patients, but a tear mid-procedure can wait until the appointment ends

distractorExplanations.a: Washing gloves degrades the material and causes wicking; exam gloves are single-use and must be replaced between patients.
distractorExplanations.b: Session-based glove use carries contamination from one patient to the next; gloves are changed for every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: A torn glove is no longer a barrier, so it must be replaced promptly during the procedure, not at the end of the appointment.

options.a: After removing gloves, but not before donning a new pair
options.b: Before donning gloves; glove removal itself leaves hands clean
options.c: At the start of each session and whenever hands look soiled
options.d: Before donning gloves and after removing gloves

distractorExplanations.a: Skips hand hygiene before gloving; contaminated hands transfer microbes onto the outside of new gloves as they are put on.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands are contaminated during glove removal and through glove micro-tears, so hand hygiene is required after removal too.
distractorExplanations.c: Session-start hygiene skips the per-patient moments around glove use; invisible contamination still requires hand hygiene.

danb-ice-readiness-check-standard-precau.explanation: Hand hygiene is the core of standard precautions and is needed around glove use. Hand hygiene is also required whenever hands are visibly soiled.

options.a: Protect mucous membranes of the wearer from splash/spatter
options.b: Protect the wearer from airborne TB droplet nuclei in place of an N95 respirator
options.c: Protect the patient from the wearer's droplets, with no role in staff protection
options.d: Serve as eye and face protection without the need for separate eyewear

distractorExplanations.b: A surgical mask is not a respirator; airborne TB exposure calls for a fit-tested N95 or higher, not a surgical mask.
distractorExplanations.c: Under OSHA the mask is PPE for the wearer's nose and mouth against spatter; source control for the patient is a secondary benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: A mask covers only the nose and mouth; eyes still need goggles or a face shield when spatter is anticipated.

danb-ice-readiness-check-standard-precau.explanation: Masks are PPE for splash/droplet; they are not sterilizers and are not week-long single items. It also reduces the wearer's droplet exposure.

options.a: During surgical procedures, but not during routine hygiene or restorative care
options.b: When splash or spatter of blood/saliva is reasonably anticipated
options.c: By the operator only, since the assistant sits outside the spatter zone
options.d: When the patient has a known infectious disease noted in the medical history

distractorExplanations.a: Ultrasonic scaling, handpieces, and air-water syringes create spatter during routine care, so eye protection is not limited to surgery.
distractorExplanations.c: The assistant is within the spatter range of the oral cavity and needs eye protection just like the operator.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard Precautions do not depend on disclosed disease; eye protection is driven by anticipated splash, not by the health history.

options.a: Pull a second glove over the torn one and finish the procedure
options.b: Disinfect the torn glove with alcohol and continue if the skin is not cut
options.c: Remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and don new gloves before continuing
options.d: Finish the current step, then change gloves without hand hygiene in between

distractorExplanations.a: Double-gloving over a tear keeps a contaminated glove and skips hand hygiene; the torn glove must come off first.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol degrades glove material and does not restore the barrier; a torn glove is removed, hands cleaned, and new gloves donned.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying the change keeps hands exposed, and skipping hand hygiene before regloving contaminates the new gloves.

options.a: Disinfect instruments so they need no further sterilization
options.b: Remove debris via cavitation before sterilization
options.c: Remove debris after sterilization, before instruments are stored
options.d: Replace manual scrubbing and the need for utility gloves

distractorExplanations.a: Ultrasonic cleaning removes debris but is not a disinfection or sterilization step; critical and semicritical items still go to the sterilizer.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the sequence: debris must be removed before packaging and sterilization because bioburden shields microbes from the sterilant.
distractorExplanations.d: Ultrasonics reduce hand scrubbing, but puncture-resistant utility gloves are still required when loading and unloading the basket.

options.a: Allowing instruments to skip cleaning because cassettes shield them from debris
options.b: Serving as the sterilization wrap so no pouch or wrap is needed in the autoclave
options.c: Keeping sets together and reducing sharps handling injuries during processing
options.d: Reducing the need for chemical indicators inside each wrapped set

distractorExplanations.a: Cassettes hold instruments during processing, but the instruments inside still go through ultrasonic or washer cleaning.
distractorExplanations.b: Most cassettes are perforated and must still be wrapped or pouched to maintain sterility after the cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Each wrapped cassette still needs an internal chemical indicator; cassettes organize sets but do not replace process monitoring.

options.a: That the sterilizer killed spores, so weekly biological monitoring can be skipped
options.b: That the load is sterile once the external tape changes color, without other checks
options.c: That the instruments were cleaned of bioburden before packaging
options.d: That sterilizing conditions were present—not necessarily that every item is sterile

distractorExplanations.a: Spore kill is verified only by biological indicators; chemical indicators do not replace weekly spore testing.
distractorExplanations.b: External tape only shows the package went through a cycle; it does not prove sterility of the contents.
distractorExplanations.c: Chemical indicators respond to sterilizer conditions, not to cleaning quality; residual debris is checked by inspection.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: External/internal chemical indicators are process monitors; biologic indicators verify sterilizer kill. Each indicator responds to the specific parameters (e.g., temperature/steam exposure) it is designed for.

options.a: At least weekly to verify sterilizer lethality
options.b: Once a month, with chemical indicators covering the weeks between tests
options.c: Only after sterilizer repairs, with chemical indicators used day to day
options.d: Quarterly, as required for steam sterilizers under OSHA rules

distractorExplanations.b: Monthly testing is below the CDC weekly minimum, and chemical indicators cannot substitute for spore testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Spore testing after repairs is required in addition to, not instead of, routine weekly biological monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: CDC (not OSHA) sets the at-least-weekly biological monitoring guidance; quarterly testing is far too infrequent.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: CDC recommends routine BI monitoring; implant loads need BI results before use when required. CDC also calls for a biological indicator with every load containing an implantable device.

options.a: Rerun the spore test and keep using the sterilizer while awaiting the result
options.b: Take the sterilizer out of service and do not use loads until failures are resolved
options.c: Recall only loads containing implants and keep processing other instruments
options.d: Switch to a chemical vapor cycle on the same unit without investigating the failure

distractorExplanations.a: CDC calls for removing the sterilizer from service while the failure is retested and investigated, not continued use.
distractorExplanations.c: A positive BI means every load since the last negative test may be unsterile; recall is not limited to implant loads.
distractorExplanations.d: The failure must be investigated (loading, cycle parameters, equipment) before the unit is used again in any cycle.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: Failed BI indicates possible sterilization failure—quarantine and investigate. Recall and reprocess affected loads per policy.

options.a: Used for routine processing of unwrapped handpieces between patients
options.b: Used for implant trays, which can then be stored wrapped for later use
options.c: Used only for emergencies when no sterile replacement exists
options.d: Used in place of precleaning when an instrument is needed quickly

distractorExplanations.a: Routine use of immediate-use sterilization to cover short inventory is discouraged; it is for urgent situations only.
distractorExplanations.b: Implants should not be flash-sterilized, and immediate-use items are used right away rather than stored.
distractorExplanations.d: Instruments must be cleaned before any sterilization cycle, including immediate-use cycles; debris blocks steam contact.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: IUSS is for urgent situations with strict controls—not routine processing. It is not a routine convenience or a substitute for adequate inventory.

options.a: Packed tightly and stacked flat to maximize each cycle's load
options.b: Laid flat with pouches stacked plastic side down in layers
options.c: Loaded with cassettes touching the chamber walls to use all space
options.d: Arranged to allow steam/air circulation—not overloaded or stacked

distractorExplanations.a: Overloading and flat stacking block steam penetration and drying, a common cause of sterilization failure and wet packs.
distractorExplanations.b: Pouches should stand on edge or be spaced so steam reaches the paper side; stacked layers trap air and moisture.
distractorExplanations.c: Packages touching the chamber walls impede circulation and can get wet or overheated; leave space per the IFU.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: Steam must contact all surfaces; follow manufacturer loading instructions. Follow the sterilizer and packaging IFU so steam can penetrate every package.

options.a: Open/unlocked so sterilant contacts joint surfaces
options.b: Closed and locked at the first ratchet to protect the tips
options.c: Closed after ultrasonic cleaning so joints stay free of debris
options.d: Disassembled only if they have a box lock, otherwise left closed

distractorExplanations.b: Even one locked ratchet keeps the joint closed, so steam cannot reach the box-lock surfaces; hinges must be open.
distractorExplanations.c: Closing hinges after cleaning blocks sterilant at the joint; they are cleaned and sterilized in the open position.
distractorExplanations.d: All hinged instruments are processed open or unlocked; box-lock design does not change the open-hinge rule.

options.a: Sterilize heat-sensitive items that cannot go in the autoclave
options.b: Clean instruments after packaging, just before the autoclave cycle
options.c: Disinfect instruments so staff can handle them without utility gloves
options.d: Remove debris via cavitation before packaging/sterilization

distractorExplanations.a: Ultrasonic cavitation cleans; it does not sterilize, and heat-sensitive items need HLD or a low-temperature sterilant.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleaning happens before packaging; once sealed in a pouch, instruments cannot be cleaned by the ultrasonic unit.
distractorExplanations.c: Ultrasonic cleaning is not disinfection, and utility gloves remain required when handling contaminated instruments.

options.a: That sterilizer process conditions for that indicator type were met
options.b: That instruments are sterile and ready for implant procedures
options.c: That spores were killed, replacing weekly biological monitoring
options.d: That instruments were cleaned and free of bioburden before packaging

distractorExplanations.b: Implant loads need a negative biological indicator before release; a chemical indicator does not prove sterility.
distractorExplanations.c: Only biological indicators test spore kill; chemical indicators supplement but never replace weekly spore testing.
distractorExplanations.d: Indicators react to sterilizer conditions such as temperature and steam, not to how well instruments were cleaned.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: Indicators monitor process conditions; biologic monitoring verifies sterilizer performance on a schedule. A chemical indicator alone does not prove the items are sterile.

options.a: Sterilized closed on the first ratchet to keep tips aligned
options.b: Sterilized in the open/unlocked position
options.c: Sterilized closed, then opened after the cycle to dry the joints
options.d: Wrapped closed inside a cassette that holds them in position

distractorExplanations.a: Any locked ratchet keeps the joint closed and blocks steam at the hinge; tip alignment does not justify locking.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening after the cycle is too late: the joint surfaces were never exposed to the sterilant during the cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Cassettes hold hinged instruments open; packaging them closed prevents sterilant contact with the joint.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: Open position improves sterilant contact on hinges. Open hinges let the sterilant contact all surfaces.

options.a: Dried on the counter, then stored as sterile if the indicator changed
options.b: Used first, the same day, before contamination can wick through
options.c: Considered compromised for sterility assurance and reprocessed
options.d: Accepted if the internal chemical indicator shows a full color change

distractorExplanations.a: Moisture lets microbes wick through the wrap; drying afterward does not restore sterility, even with a passed indicator.
distractorExplanations.b: A wet pack is treated as contaminated immediately; using it quickly does not make it sterile.
distractorExplanations.d: The indicator shows the cycle conditions were met but says nothing about contamination wicking through a wet wrap.

danb-ice-readiness-check-instrument-proc.explanation: Wet packs can wick contaminants; reprocess. Reprocess per protocol.

options.a: Barrier-protected and/or cleaned and disinfected between patients
options.b: Sterilized with a chemical sterilant at the start of each day
options.c: Wiped with a disinfectant only when blood is visible on them
options.d: Cleaned with soap and water between patients without disinfecting

distractorExplanations.b: Sterilants and high-level disinfectants are not for environmental surfaces, and once-daily treatment misses between-patient turnover.
distractorExplanations.c: Clinical contact surfaces are contaminated by spatter and gloved hands even without visible blood; treat them every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning removes soil but clinical contact surfaces also need an EPA-registered disinfectant when not barrier-protected.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Between-patient surface asepsis prevents cross-infection. Use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

options.a: Disinfection between patients with a tuberculocidal product, like clinical contact surfaces
options.b: Routine cleaning; disinfection when contaminated with blood/body fluids
options.c: Weekly cleaning, since floors are not involved in disease transmission
options.d: Daily high-level disinfection with glutaraldehyde-based floor solutions

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses housekeeping surfaces with clinical contact surfaces; floors and walls need routine cleaning, not per-patient disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: Housekeeping surfaces carry low risk but still need regular (usually daily) cleaning and prompt disinfection of blood spills.
distractorExplanations.d: High-level disinfectants such as glutaraldehyde are for semicritical devices and are not used on environmental surfaces.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Housekeeping surfaces are lower risk but still need cleaning and targeted disinfection when soiled. Follow office policy for frequency.

options.a: Changed at the end of each day unless they become visibly soiled
options.b: Wiped with disinfectant between patients and reused while intact
options.c: Changed between patients and surfaces cleaned if contamination occurred
options.d: Replaced between patients by staff still wearing contaminated gloves

distractorExplanations.a: Barriers are single-patient items; leaving one in place all day carries contamination from patient to patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Barrier film is meant to be discarded after each patient; wiping it does not reliably decontaminate and defeats its purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: Remove barriers with gloved hands, then remove gloves and perform hand hygiene before placing new barriers with clean hands.

options.a: Is sterile water for routine restorative care as well as for surgical irrigation
options.b: Meets potable standards once lines are flushed for 2 minutes each morning
options.c: Is safe once the unit's antiretraction valves are working properly
options.d: Meets drinking-water standards for routine care (≤500 CFU/mL heterotrophic bacteria)

distractorExplanations.a: Sterile water is required for surgical procedures; routine nonsurgical care needs water meeting drinking-water standards.
distractorExplanations.b: Flushing temporarily lowers counts but does not remove biofilm; waterline treatment and monitoring are still required.
distractorExplanations.c: Antiretraction valves prevent suck-back of oral fluids but do nothing to control biofilm in the waterlines.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: DUWL maintenance and monitoring reduce biofilm risks; sterile water is required for certain surgical irrigations. That ≤500 CFU/mL figure is the common benchmark, maintained through monitoring and maintenance.

options.a: Any item that touched the patient's mouth, including lightly stained gauze
options.b: Sharps and items saturated with blood/saliva that drip when compressed
options.c: All gloves and masks used chairside, even if not saturated with blood
options.d: Extracted teeth containing amalgam, which go in the red biohazard bag

distractorExplanations.a: Lightly soiled gauze is generally ordinary waste; regulated waste is sharps and items that release blood or saliva when compressed.
distractorExplanations.c: Used gloves and masks that are not saturated are usually general waste; red-bagging everything inflates cost without a rule basis.
distractorExplanations.d: Amalgam teeth must not go in red bags destined for incineration, which releases mercury; they are handled as amalgam waste.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Regulated waste definitions are specific—sharps and saturated infectious items; follow local rules. Definitions vary, so follow local regulations.

options.a: Placed in the red biohazard bag for medical-waste incineration
options.b: Heat-sterilized before being returned to the patient or donated to a dental school
options.c: Handled as potential biohazard and amalgam-containing waste per EPA/state rules
options.d: Placed in the sharps container with used needles and blades

distractorExplanations.a: Medical-waste incineration vaporizes the mercury in amalgam, so amalgam-containing teeth stay out of red-bag incineration.
distractorExplanations.b: CDC advises against heat-sterilizing amalgam teeth because heat releases mercury vapor; formalin immersion is used for school use.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharps containers are usually incinerated or autoclaved, both of which can release mercury from amalgam restorations.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Amalgam/mercury disposal has special environmental rules; treated teeth may be returned under policies. They must not be incinerated as ordinary trash, which vaporizes mercury.

options.a: PPE, then disinfectant sprayed on the blood and wiped off immediately
options.b: Absorbent removal, then a quick wipe with 70% alcohol as the disinfectant
options.c: PPE, then a sterilant such as glutaraldehyde applied to the counter
options.d: PPE, absorbent removal of bulk soil, then EPA-registered disinfectant

distractorExplanations.a: Skips removal of bulk blood and ignores contact time; organic soil inactivates disinfectant and immediate wiping prevents kill.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol evaporates before achieving contact time and is not recommended by CDC as a surface disinfectant for blood spills.
distractorExplanations.c: Sterilants and high-level disinfectants are not intended for environmental surfaces; use an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Clean then disinfect with proper wet time. Leave the disinfectant wet for its labeled contact time.

options.a: Disinfection reduces pathogens; sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores
options.b: High-level disinfection and sterilization both kill spores reliably at standard contact times
options.c: Sterilization reduces pathogens to safe levels; disinfection destroys all microbial life on items
options.d: Disinfection destroys spores given enough contact time; sterilization just shortens the process

distractorExplanations.b: High-level disinfection kills most microbes but not high numbers of bacterial spores at standard contact times; only sterilization does.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the definitions: disinfection reduces pathogens, while sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores.
distractorExplanations.d: Surface disinfectants are not sporicidal at labeled times; sterilization is a different level of kill, not a faster disinfection.

options.a: Disinfecting housekeeping surfaces such as floors before clinical surfaces
options.b: Removing barriers, cleaning/disinfecting clinical contact surfaces
options.c: Spraying surfaces with disinfectant and placing barriers before wiping
options.d: Wiping surfaces with a dry towel, then covering them with fresh barriers

distractorExplanations.a: Floors and walls are low-risk housekeeping surfaces; between-patient priority is clinical contact surfaces and barriers.
distractorExplanations.c: Surfaces must be precleaned and the disinfectant left for its contact time before new barriers go on.
distractorExplanations.d: Dry wiping does not disinfect; contaminated surfaces need cleaning and an EPA-registered disinfectant before re-barriering.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Systematic between-patient IPC protects the next patient. Sharps and waste are also managed safely during turnover.

options.a: Disinfected once at day's end if no blood was visible during care
options.b: Covered with barriers, which are left in place for the full day
options.c: Barrier-protected and/or cleaned and disinfected between patients
options.d: Sprayed with disinfectant and covered with a barrier without precleaning

distractorExplanations.a: Spatter and gloved-hand contact contaminate surfaces with every patient, visible blood or not; treat them between patients.
distractorExplanations.b: Barriers are changed between patients; a day-long barrier carries contamination from one patient to the next.
distractorExplanations.d: Precleaning removes organic soil that inactivates disinfectant; spray-and-cover skips both cleaning and contact time.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: CDC/OSAP-aligned practice: barriers and/or disinfection between patients. Use an appropriate EPA-registered product.

options.a: Disinfection between every patient with an intermediate-level product
options.b: Monthly cleaning, since they rarely contact patients' hands
options.c: The same EPA hospital disinfectant schedule as clinical contact surfaces
options.d: Routine cleaning; more frequent disinfection when visibly soiled

distractorExplanations.a: Per-patient intermediate-level disinfection is the rule for clinical contact surfaces, not for floors and walls.
distractorExplanations.b: Low contact does not mean monthly; housekeeping surfaces are cleaned on a regular schedule and when soiled.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the two surface categories; housekeeping surfaces need routine cleaning, not the clinical between-patient schedule.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Housekeeping surfaces are cleaned routinely; intensive disinfection when soiled. Disinfect promptly when soiled with blood or body fluids.

options.a: Meets dental water standards (eg, ≤500 CFU/mL heterotrophic bacteria for non-surgical use)
options.b: Is sterile for every procedure because tap water cannot be used in dental units
options.c: Is acceptable once lines are flushed for 20–30 seconds at the start of each clinic day
options.d: Is checked by the unit's in-line filter, which removes the need for water testing

distractorExplanations.b: Sterile water is required only for surgical procedures; nonsurgical care uses water meeting the ≤500 CFU/mL standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Flushing helps but does not eliminate biofilm; CDC still expects waterline treatment and periodic monitoring.
distractorExplanations.d: In-line filters reduce bacteria but can fail or be colonized; monitoring is still needed to confirm water quality.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Waterline biofilms need active management and monitoring. Flushing and waterline treatment protocols maintain that level.

options.a: Recapped with two hands and placed in a red bag with gauze
options.b: Placed in appropriate puncture-resistant containers
options.c: Placed in a sealed red bag lined with a second plastic bag
options.d: Collected in an empty plastic bottle, then sealed in the regular trash

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is prohibited, and red bags are not puncture-resistant enough to contain sharps.
distractorExplanations.c: Double bags still tear on needles and blades; sharps require closable, leak-proof, puncture-resistant containers.
distractorExplanations.d: Improvised bottles are not labeled sharps containers, and regulated sharps waste cannot go in ordinary trash.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Sharps and regulated waste have specific containment/disposal rules. Handle and dispose of them per OSHA and state rules.

options.a: Disinfect with a low-level product first, then clean up the remaining blood afterward
options.b: Wipe with a damp towel, then apply a sterilant such as glutaraldehyde
options.c: Contain, clean, and disinfect with an appropriate intermediate-level disinfectant
options.d: Cover with a barrier film and disinfect at the end of the clinic day

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the order (clean first, then disinfect) and uses low-level instead of intermediate-level disinfectant for blood.
distractorExplanations.b: Sterilants are for semicritical devices, not environmental surfaces; spills need an EPA-registered intermediate-level product.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood spills are cleaned and disinfected promptly; covering them leaves infectious material on the surface.

danb-ice-readiness-check-environmental-0.explanation: Blood spills need proper cleaning/disinfection. Follow the office protocol for spills.

options.a: Establish an exposure control plan, offer HBV vaccination, provide PPE, and train employees
options.b: Establish an exposure control plan and require HBV vaccination as a condition of hire
options.c: Provide PPE and annual training, with HBV vaccination costs paid by the employee
options.d: Train employees every three years and review the exposure control plan as needed

distractorExplanations.b: OSHA requires HBV vaccine to be offered free, and employees may decline by signing a declination; it cannot be a hiring condition.
distractorExplanations.c: The employer must offer HBV vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: BBP training is required at assignment and annually, and the exposure control plan must be reviewed at least annually.

options.a: Squeeze the site to bleed it, apply bleach, and report at the end of the day
options.b: Wash the site, report immediately, and follow post-exposure evaluation
options.c: Wash the site, then report only if the patient's history shows HIV or hepatitis
options.d: Wash the site and start PEP within 7 days if the source tests positive

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing and caustic agents are not recommended, and reporting must be immediate so PEP can start within hours.
distractorExplanations.c: Every exposure is reported regardless of the source history, since infection status is often unknown or undisclosed.
distractorExplanations.d: HIV PEP should start within hours (ideally within 2, no later than 72); waiting up to a week is far too late.

danb-ice-readiness-check-occupational-00.explanation: Timely reporting enables PEP decisions and documentation. Prophylaxis decisions follow the post-exposure protocol.

options.a: Bloodborne exposure procedures and post-exposure follow-up steps
options.b: Sterilizer cycle parameters and biological monitoring results
options.c: Hazard labels for secondary containers, replacing the written HazCom program
options.d: Hazard information and safe handling/PPE guidance for chemicals

distractorExplanations.a: Those belong in the exposure control plan under the BBP Standard, not in chemical Safety Data Sheets.
distractorExplanations.b: Cycle parameters and spore test results are kept in sterilization logs, not on Safety Data Sheets.
distractorExplanations.c: SDS supplement but do not replace container labels or the written Hazard Communication program.

options.a: Recapping only with a one-handed scoop technique
options.b: Installing sharps containers at the point of use in each operatory
options.c: Using a safety syringe with a self-sheathing needle
options.d: Wearing puncture-resistant utility gloves during instrument cleanup

distractorExplanations.b: A sharps container is an engineering control that isolates the hazard, not a change in how the task is performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Safer sharps devices are engineering controls built into equipment; work-practice controls change worker behavior.
distractorExplanations.d: Utility gloves are personal protective equipment, a separate category from work-practice controls.

danb-ice-readiness-check-occupational-00.explanation: Work-practice controls change how tasks are performed to reduce exposure. Two-handed recapping is not acceptable; a safer mechanical method may also be used.

options.a: Available in the sterilization area, with squeeze bottles elsewhere instead
options.b: Available, accessible, and flushed/maintained per requirements
options.c: Located within a one-minute walk and flushed once each month
options.d: Installed at a sink and tested once a year during the OSHA review

distractorExplanations.a: Squeeze bottles are supplemental only and do not meet the required flushing flow or duration of a plumbed eyewash.
distractorExplanations.c: ANSI Z358.1 calls for reaching the station in about 10 seconds and activating plumbed units weekly.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual testing is far too infrequent; plumbed eyewashes are activated weekly to flush the line and verify flow.

danb-ice-readiness-check-occupational-00.explanation: Prompt irrigation capability is required for chemical exposures. This applies where corrosive chemicals are used.

options.a: Turning off the scavenger during induction so the patient receives full flow
options.b: Checking equipment for leaks once a year, without a scavenging system
options.c: Scavenging systems, equipment checks, and appropriate ventilation/work practices
options.d: Room air purifiers with HEPA filters placed near the dental chair

distractorExplanations.a: Scavenging is needed throughout administration; switching it off releases exhaled nitrous into the operatory.
distractorExplanations.b: Leak checks are done regularly but do not replace scavenging, which captures exhaled gas at the source.
distractorExplanations.d: HEPA filters trap particles, not gases; they do not remove nitrous oxide from room air.

options.a: Hazard communication labeling, SDS use, and chemical spill cleanup
options.b: Fire extinguisher use, evacuation routes, and emergency action plans
options.c: Radiation safety, film handling, and dosimeter badge procedures
options.d: Modes of transmission, PPE use, and exposure response

distractorExplanations.a: Those are Hazard Communication Standard topics; BBP training covers bloodborne transmission, PPE, and exposure response.
distractorExplanations.b: Those fall under OSHA's emergency action and fire prevention rules, not the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Radiation safety is governed by state radiation rules, not the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens training requirement.

danb-ice-readiness-check-occupational-00.explanation: BBP training covers exposure prevention and response; employers document training. Training also covers engineering and work-practice controls, and it must be documented.

options.a: Labeled/color-coded, closable, and suitable to contain contents without leakage
options.b: Labeled and closable, with clear bags acceptable for bloody gauze
options.c: Color-coded and filled to the very top before sealing to reduce waste-hauling costs
options.d: Lined with regular trash bags as long as the outer bin is labeled

distractorExplanations.b: Regulated waste bags must be red or carry the biohazard label; clear bags hide the hazard from handlers.
distractorExplanations.c: Overfilling past the fill line causes punctures and spills; containers are sealed and replaced before they are full.
distractorExplanations.d: The liner itself must be red or biohazard-labeled so the waste stays identified once removed from the bin.

options.a: Patients with latent TB infection should be treated in airborne isolation rooms
options.b: Patients with infectious TB should have elective care deferred
options.c: Patients with active TB can be treated routinely if staff wear surgical masks
options.d: Elective care can proceed once a patient with active TB has started medication

distractorExplanations.a: Latent TB infection is not contagious; airborne precautions are for suspected or confirmed active TB disease.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgical masks do not filter TB droplet nuclei; active TB calls for deferral or treatment with N95 respirators and airborne precautions.
distractorExplanations.d: Starting treatment is not enough; elective care waits until a physician confirms the patient is no longer infectious.

danb-ice-readiness-check-occupational-01.explanation: Airborne TB requires special handling beyond Standard Precautions alone. Urgent care uses airborne precautions or referral as appropriate.

options.a: Establish an exposure control plan and require HBV titers before hiring
options.b: Offer HBV vaccination within 30 days of hire and review the plan every five years
options.c: Establish an exposure control plan and offer HBV vaccination to at-risk employees
options.d: Keep exposure records only for the length of each employee's employment

distractorExplanations.a: OSHA requires offering HBV vaccination after assignment, not pre-hire titers; post-vaccination titer testing is a CDC follow-up.
distractorExplanations.b: The vaccine is offered within 10 working days of assignment, and the exposure control plan is reviewed at least annually.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA requires exposure and medical records to be kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years.

options.a: Apply bleach to the wound, then report the incident after the shift ends
options.b: Milk the wound to force bleeding, then report if the patient is high risk
options.c: Wash the site and get tested in 6 months before filing a report
options.d: Wash the site, report promptly, and follow post-exposure evaluation protocol

distractorExplanations.a: Caustics like bleach damage tissue and are not recommended; delayed reporting can push PEP past its effective window.
distractorExplanations.b: Squeezing is not recommended, and every exposure must be reported regardless of the source patient's perceived risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Baseline testing and PEP decisions happen right after exposure; waiting months to report defeats post-exposure follow-up.

options.a: Sharps containers and safer needle devices
options.b: Hand hygiene and one-handed needle recapping
options.c: Gloves, masks, and protective eyewear
options.d: Written exposure control plans and staff training

distractorExplanations.b: Hand hygiene and the scoop technique change how a task is done, which makes them work-practice controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves, masks, and eyewear are personal protective equipment, the last line of defense rather than engineering controls.
distractorExplanations.d: Plans and training are administrative controls; engineering controls physically isolate or remove the hazard.

options.a: Using a nasal hood without scavenging, at lower flow rates
options.b: Scavenging systems, good ventilation, and equipment checks for leaks
options.c: Letting the patient talk and mouth-breathe during nitrous sedation
options.d: Opening a window and relying on room fans instead of a scavenger

distractorExplanations.a: Lower flow does not replace scavenging; without it exhaled nitrous oxide escapes into the operatory air.
distractorExplanations.c: Talking and mouth breathing release nitrous oxide into the room; patients should be discouraged from talking during sedation.
distractorExplanations.d: General ventilation supplements but cannot replace a scavenging system that captures gas at the source.

options.a: Switch to powder-free latex gloves, which contain no latex proteins
options.b: Wear cotton liners under latex gloves as the main precaution
options.c: Use appropriate non-latex alternatives and follow facility allergy protocols
options.d: Use vinyl gloves for patient care and latex utility gloves for instrument cleanup

distractorExplanations.a: Powder-free latex gloves still contain latex proteins; they reduce airborne allergen but are not safe for allergic staff.
distractorExplanations.b: Liners reduce irritant dermatitis but do not prevent latex-protein allergic reactions; avoiding latex is the key step.
distractorExplanations.d: Latex utility gloves still expose an allergic worker; non-latex alternatives are needed for every task.
